title: Bildad: Does God Pervert Justice?
summary: Bildad, the second friend, answers Job bluntly. God never perverts justice, so Job's children must have died for their own sin, and if Job is pure and seeks God he will be restored. Bildad appeals to the wisdom of past generations and to pictures from nature: the plant without water withers, the godless trust a spider's web, but God will yet fill the blameless with laughter.
story: Job has just ended his first reply by accusing God of watching him like a guard and refusing to pardon him (chapter 7). Bildad cannot let that stand. His speech opens the pattern that will shape the long middle of the book: three rounds of debate in which each friend speaks and Job answers. Eliphaz, the first friend, claimed a private revelation in the night (4:12-21). Bildad claims something different, the authority of tradition. His argument is simpler and harsher than Eliphaz's, and it forces into the open the conviction all three friends share: suffering is always the sign of sin, and prosperity is the reward of righteousness. The reader knows from chapters 1 and 2 that this is not why Job is suffering, and that gap between what the reader knows and what the friends assume gives every speech its tension.
historical:
Bildad is called the Shuhite. The name may connect him with Shuah, one of the sons Abraham had by Keturah, whose descendants were sent to the east (Genesis 25:1-6), though the link is not certain. Like Job and the other friends, Bildad belongs to the peoples east of Israel, and the book presents all of them as men who know and speak of God without being Israelites. The book's world is international wisdom, not Israel's temple or covenant history; Moses, the exodus, and Jerusalem are never mentioned.

That international setting fits what is known of ancient wisdom literature. Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Israel all produced collections of proverbs and reflections on how life works, and these writers shared many assumptions, above all that the world is ordered so that wise and righteous living tends to prosper. A Babylonian poem often called the Babylonian Theodicy, from roughly the early first millennium BC, stages a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend who defends the gods' justice, a form strikingly like Job's debates.
cultural:
Bildad's appeal to past generations (verses 8-10) reflects how wisdom was carried in the ancient world. Knowledge was inherited from fathers and elders, tested over many lifetimes, and a young person's experience counted for little against it. When Bildad says “we were born yesterday and know nothing,” he means that any one lifetime is too short to overturn what the ancestors learned.

His pictures come from the world of the riverbank and the garden. Papyrus and reeds grew thick in the marshes of the Nile and in wet ground elsewhere in the region; cut off from water, they withered fast. The spider's web (verse 14) is a picture of something that looks like shelter but gives way under weight. The tent of the wicked (verse 22) reflects a world where many lived in tents, and a tent was the household itself: its family, goods, and future.
literary: Bildad's speech is carefully arranged. Verses 2-7 state his thesis and apply it to Job directly: God is just, Job's children sinned, and Job should seek God and be restored. Verses 8-10 give his source, the tradition of the fathers. Verses 11-19 illustrate the thesis with two plant images, the papyrus that withers without water and a flourishing plant that is uprooted and forgotten. Verses 20-22 return to the thesis and close with a promise of laughter and joy. The speech is framed by a question about Job's words (“How long will you go on saying such things?”) and ends on the tent of the wicked, a quiet warning about which side Job may be on. Like much wisdom poetry, it moves by parallel lines, rhetorical questions, and images from nature.

outline.t: God is just: seek him and be restored
The withering plant and the spider's web
God will not reject the blameless

doctrines.note: Bildad is right that God does not pervert justice, a truth the whole Bible affirms. His error is to read every event as a direct and immediate verdict, so that suffering proves guilt. The book of Job as a whole rejects that equation while keeping the conviction that God is just.

Bildad's reliance on tradition shows both the strength and the limit of inherited wisdom. Proverbs states general patterns about how life usually goes; Job shows what happens when those patterns are turned into rules without exceptions.
Bildad calls Job to seek God and plead for mercy, which is sound counsel in itself. What makes it wrong here is the assumption that Job has a hidden sin that explains his losses.

words.note: Mishpat, justice, judgment, or what is right. It can mean a court's verdict, a legal case, or the right order of things. Bildad uses it in verse 3 to defend God. Job will soon use the same legal vocabulary to ask for his own day in court, so the word frames the whole debate.

Shaddai, usually translated Almighty. It is an old divine name, used in Genesis with the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1) and especially often in Job, where it appears more than in any other book. Its precise origin is debated; the traditional rendering stresses God's power.

Dor, generation. Bildad appeals to the former generation and the discoveries of their fathers (verse 8). The word carries the sense of a long chain of human experience, which Bildad treats as a court of appeal higher than one man's complaint.

Tam, blameless, complete, or whole. It is the word the narrator uses of Job in 1:1 and that God uses of him in 1:8 and 2:3. When Bildad says God does not reject the blameless (verse 20), the reader knows that God has already called Job exactly that.

christ: The link here is by way of contrast. Bildad's logic, that disaster reveals sin, was still alive in Jesus' day. When his disciples asked whether a man was born blind because of his own sin or his parents', Jesus answered that it was neither (John 9:1-3). When people told him of Galileans killed by Pilate, and he recalled eighteen killed when a tower fell in Siloam, he denied that they were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1-5). Most sharply, the one the New Testament presents as truly righteous suffered the worst death of all, and onlookers read his suffering as proof that God had rejected him (Matthew 27:41-43). The cross breaks Bildad's equation for good: the blameless one was not spared, and God vindicated him afterward in the resurrection.

hard.q: Did Job's children die because of their sins, as Bildad says?
hard.a: Bildad states it plainly in verse 4: “When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion.” It is one of the cruelest lines in the book, spoken to a grieving father. The reader knows from chapter 1 that the children's deaths came in the heavenly test of Job, not as punishment. Job had even offered sacrifices in case his children had sinned in their hearts (1:5). Bildad's claim is therefore a deduction from his theory, not something he knows. At the end, God says the friends have not spoken what is right about him (42:7). Readers should be careful not to treat Bildad's words as the Bible's teaching simply because they appear in the Bible. Job records the friends' speeches in order to test them, and many of their claims are shown to be wrong in the way they apply true principles to Job's case.

questions: Bildad says true things about God's justice but applies them wrongly to Job. How can we tell the difference between a true principle and a true principle misapplied?
Bildad trusts the wisdom of past generations. Where is that trust healthy, and where can it keep us from seeing what is in front of us?
If you have ever heard someone explain another person's tragedy as a punishment, how did it land? What would have been better to say?
